autoResolved.choice: Whether the method-level caller check reads context.ContainingSymbol, walks syntax ancestors, or calls SemanticModel.GetEnclosingSymbol.
autoResolved.resolution: CompositionPoint.IsInsideContainerFactory(SemanticModel, position, CancellationToken) calls GetEnclosingSymbol and tests the result with IsContainerFactory. No syntax ancestor walk, and no ContainingSymbol read at any consumer.
autoResolved.principle: rails-dry-code rail 8 — 'When work needs a capability a BCL, OS, or OSS primitive already provides, default to reusing that primitive… A tested BCL/OS/OSS primitive was reimplemented from scratch or hand-composed from lower-level calls to avoid giving it an owner' is the Violation; the one-owner rule is the forcing function to pick CompositionPoint, not a bar to reuse. Reinforced by best-practices guide 6a, 'Never scaffold or wire a check to pass.'
autoResolved.evidence: Judge's probe on Roslyn 4.14.0 through CompilationWithAnalyzers, five positions: direct in Create() → GetEnclosingSymbol Method:Sub.Host.Create()/Ordinary (permit); inside a lambda in Create() → Method:lambda expression/AnonymousFunction (report, Acceptance 12); inside a local function in Create() → Method:Nested()/LocalFunction (report, Acceptance 12); another method → that method (report); a cref in Create()'s doc comment → NamedType:Sub.Host (report). context.ContainingSymbol returns Method:Create for the first FOUR of those, so it permits the Acceptance-12 bypass. The syntax-walk alternative hand-composes what GetEnclosingSymbol already computes, and is additionally wrong-by-accident on the trivia case: the .Parent chain from a cref terminates at SingleLineDocumentationCommentTrivia and never reaches MethodDeclaration. GetEnclosingSymbol has zero uses in the analyzer project today, so giving it one deliberate owner costs nothing.

autoResolved.choice: Whether WrittenNameScanner writes its own name resolution or the two-tier mechanic AttributeIdentity already owns is extracted into one owner.
autoResolved.resolution: Extract: WrittenNameScanner.RecoverBoundType holds the GetTypeInfo tier, and AttributeIdentity.ResolveAttributeType calls it while keeping its own tier 1 (constructor → containing type) and its syntactic …Attribute fallback. AG0008 and AG0105 behaviour is unchanged.
autoResolved.principle: rails-dry-code rail 4 ('a capability ruled "reuse" calls the existing owner; one ruled "extract" collapses the copies into a single shared owner and calls it') together with rail 6 ('a duplicated block or whole function — same logic even with renamed variables').
autoResolved.evidence: AttributeIdentity.cs:60-72 is the live two-tier body, with a four-line comment stating exactly why the second tier exists. The judge measured the same recovery is required at the NAME-NODE level: for [Guarded] with the required constructor argument omitted, GetSymbolInfo returns Symbol=null with CandidateReason=OverloadResolutionFailure and CandidateSymbols=[the constructor], while GetTypeInfo returns NamedType:G.GuardedAttribute — and MemberUseScanner produces NO ObjectCreation operation for that attribute, versus one for the well-formed [Guarded(1)]. A second implementation of the tier would be a literal copy of AttributeIdentity.cs:69-71. Tier 1 is NOT shared: AttributeIdentity narrows a constructor to its type, while WrittenNameScanner must keep the symbol because AG0041 governs internal Engine MEMBERS as well as types.

Note the distinct case this does NOT cover: an UNBOUND CALL to a resolvable guarded type still reports, because the guarded TYPE node resolves even though no IInvocationOperation is produced — measured, and the reason the unbound-call fixture is a required rule.
